props.title: Black Christmas
props.initialSlug: Sorority sisters face deadly holiday stalker on campus

sections.content: Black Christmas revolutionized the slasher genre before Halloween (1978) supposedly invented it. Director Bob Clark crafted a genuinely unsettling proto-slasher that trades gore for psychological terror. The film's innovative POV killer shots influenced countless horror films, while its "calls are coming from inside the house" premise became a cultural touchstone. What sets it apart is its sophisticated approach - rather than mindless teen carnage, it explores themes of female autonomy and institutional failure while building unbearable tension through sound design and negative space.

sections.content: The film's influence extends far beyond seasonal horror. A Stranger Calls (1979) directly borrowed its telephone terror premise, while Scream (1996) paid homage with its opening phone sequence. The unseen killer Billy's deranged phone calls created a template for psychological horror that emphasizes threat through voice and suggestion rather than explicit violence. Modern films like It Follows (2014) continue this tradition of abstract menace over gore.

Clark's direction was groundbreaking for 1974, employing techniques that would become horror staples. The killer's POV shots through windows and from dark corners built suspense while keeping the threat mysterious. Halloween (1978) and Friday the 13th (1980) would later adopt these techniques as genre conventions. The film's Christmas setting also subverted expectations, turning holiday comfort into creeping dread - a approach later seen in Gremlins (1984) and Krampus (2015). SUBHEAD: Legacy and Modern Impact

sections.content: Modern horror continues drawing from Black Christmas's (1974) playbook. Films like You're Next (2011) and Ready or Not (2019) echo its themes of female protagonists fighting institutional and patriarchal threats. The original's atmospheric approach to terror influenced art-house horror like The Witch (2015) and Hereditary (2018), proving sophisticated horror can succeed without relying on jump scares and gore.
